doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Staff orchestras at ABC and the networks
summary: Wilder describes the network staff orchestras, their conductors, live broadcasts, the end of staffs by the mid-1970s, and discarded tapes.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: My goodness. We talked a bit about ABC and those must have been pretty busy days for you.
They were. They were pretty busy days for almost all the musicians in New York.
That whole thing with the orchestras, what was the era that that ran from?

I would think, well I guess it went from about the late 30’s through the 70’s. Because I think it was ‘75 when we stopped doing the Dick Cavett show, and at that point they had begun to get rid of the staff orchestras at all the networks.
They had some fairly well known classical people head up those orchestras, didn’t they?

Right. Well at NBC they got Toscannini. At CBS Paul Lavalle had the City Services Concert band, and at ABC very often we had Arthur Fiedler. And we had others, because they did the Metropolitan Opera auditions on the air, and they did “Music for a Summer Night” and “Voice of Firestone,” and they would very often have guest conductors come in for those things.
Was most of the music you recorded in those orchestra situations, was it going on tape for use later? Or was it live?

No it was live. Almost all of it was live. And a lot of it they recorded. And when they finally got rid of the staffs, all these tapes and things they had, they just threw them in the garbage. I mean a lot of them just went in the trash. And there were a couple of fellows who were involved with ABC with the library there, who had the good sense to take some of this stuff, knowing that they were just going to throw it out. And they were able to save some of it. But the bulk of it was just thrown out. And some of the libraries that © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
they had, I think they gave some of it to Columbia University or Princeton or something, and some of it was given to one of the colleges, but most of it they just threw out because it was in the way.
I’m going to return to your work ethic again — it must have served you pretty well in this situation, because it obviously had to be, there’s no crawling into the section a half hour late.

No, no, no. If you did these things it was a matter of just routine. And everybody complied. There was nothing servile about it, it was just that this was the job to do and these are the requirements for doing it.
